en: The *Continued Record of the Translation of Scriptures Past and Present*, one fascicle,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Chongfu Monastery in the West during the Gengwu year of the Kaiyuan era.
This *Record of the Translation of Scriptures* originally originated from the hall of the Translation Institute at Daci'en Monastery.
Furthermore,
the murals in this hall depict the monks and laypeople who translated the scriptures from ancient times down to the present,
beginning with Kāśyapa Mātanga and ending with the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang.
Master Mai composed an inscription for it on the wall.
From that time forth, translations and commentaries have followed one after another;
yet among all those works of literary embellishment, none contained such a record.
Although I, Sheng, am not gifted, I venture to offer this praise.
Though there may be differences between a single thread and a skein of hemp, I hope that the succession will continue without interruption.
I trust that those who read this will not find it cause for derision.

From the Supplements to the *Dàtáng Fǎnyì* (The Translation Records of the Great Tang): The śramaṇa Śākyamuni Zhītōng was rigorous and austere in his observance of the Vinaya, while being equally proficient in the sūtras and śāstras;
he paid particular attention to the gateway of dhāraṇī.
It is generally recorded that Tong left the household life during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty.
He resided at Dazongchi Monastery in the capital and harbored the aspiration to travel abroad.
He subsequently studied Sanskrit script and language at the Translation Bureau in the capital of Luoyang, quickly mastering its profound subtleties.

During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, a monk from North India arrived bearing a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Qianbi Qianyan Jing* (The Scripture of a Thousand Arms and a Thousand Eyes) to present to the court.
Emperor Wen issued an edict for Tong to collaborate with a foreign monk on the translation.
It was titled the *Qianyan Qianbi Guanshiyin Pusa Tuoluoni Shenzhou Jing* (The Divine Spell Sutra of the Thousand-Eyed, Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva),
consisting of one work in two fascicles.
Later, in the fourth year of the Yonghui era of the Heavenly Emperor (the Gui-chou year),
he again translated at Zongchi Monastery the *Qianzhuan Tuoluoni Guanshiyin Pusa Zhou Jing* (The Sūtra of the Thousand-Turned Dhāraṇī Mantra of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva) in one fascicle.
One fascicle of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s随心呪經 (Sūtra on the Mantra According to One’s Heart);
one fascicle of the Qingjing Guanshiyin Puxian Dharani Sūtra.
In total, four works comprising five fascicles.
The śramaṇa Gaovindadharma— translated into Chinese as Zūnfǎ (Venerable Dharma)—
was a native of Western India.

Translated the *Qianshou Qianyan Guanshiyin Pusa Guangda Yuanman Wuai Dabeixin Duoaloni Jing* (The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Greatly Vast, Perfect, and Unobstructed Compassionate Heart of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes), in one fascicle.
However, the title of the sūtra states it was translated by Jñānagupta of Western India.
No date is indicated.
Inferring from its provenance, it appears to be a new translation produced during the Imperial Dynasty (the Tang).
According to the preface to the *Qianbi jing* (Thousand-Armed Sūtra), it was likewise translated by Zhìtōng in collaboration with others.
The śramaṇa Ajitaghosa (translated into Chinese as Wujige [無極高]),
a native of Central India.
His learning exhausted the full range of the written word and his conduct was as pure as a perfect pearl;
he was refined in the five sciences and profoundly versed in the Tripitaka.

In the first month of the third year of the Yonghui era (the Renzi year) of Emperor Tianhuang, he arrived in Chang’an bringing a vast collection of Sanskrit texts, by imperial decree they were housed at Ci’en Monastery.
The śramaṇas, including Dasheng Cong and others— sixteen persons in total—
and the Dukes Ying and E, among others— twelve persons in total—
invited Huigao to the pagoda courtyard of Huiji Temple.
He established a maṇḍala for the Universal Assembly of Dhāraṇīs.
All requisites required for the maṇḍala were fully prepared and provided.
On the day the rite was completed, various spiritual wonders repeatedly descended.
The monastics and laypeople throughout the capital all sighed in admiration at such a rare encounter.
The śramaṇas Xuankai and others then earnestly requested that he translate the original text of this dharma.
This was subsequently carried out from the fourth year, the *guichou* year, to the fifth year, the *jiayin* year.
At Huiri Temple, he excerpted the essentials from the *Vajramahāmaṇḍala-sūtra* and compiled them into a single collection,
titled the *Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha-sūtra*, in twelve fascicles.
The śramaṇas Xuánkǎi and others recorded the dictation.
At that time, there were monks from the Mahābodhi Temple in Central India, including Ānanda, Vinayamokṣa, and the teacher Kāśyapa.
Since the *Dharmatārā-dharmaparyāya* was translated at Jingxing Monastery and compiled within the tenth fascicle of the *Ji jing* (Collected Scriptures),
it does not exist as a separate work.
The śramaṇa Nādi— translated into Chinese as Fusheng (Born of Blessings)—
is, according to the full Sanskrit term, called Pūrṇovāya.
Because his words were so voluminous, this account is merely an abbreviated and slightly corrupted version, referring to him as Nadi.
He was originally a native of Central India;
his aspirations were noble and far-reaching, and he was devoted to the propagation of the Way.
He traveled extensively throughout various kingdoms, his primary concern being to enlighten sentient beings.
He was highly proficient in the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*) and thoroughly mastered all glossaries and commentaries.
Having heard of those who sought awakening, he did not shrink from the distance of remote barbarian lands.
He once traveled to the Kingdom of Siṃhala;
furthermore, he ascended Mount Laṅkā to the southeast and journeyed through various kingdoms of the South Sea to teach and transform beings according to their conditions.
He learned that in the eastern land of China, the Mahāyāna was flourishing;
its Buddhist teachings were so magnificent that they were said to be the most eminent on Jambudvīpa.
Thereupon, he collected over five hundred fascicles of sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras from both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions, totaling more than one thousand five hundred works.
In the sixth year of the Yonghui era of the Great Emperor, it first arrived at the capital.
By imperial decree, it was ordered to be enshrined at Ci'en Monastery,
with the relevant authorities providing all necessary supplies.
In the first year of the Xianqing era,
he was commanded by imperial decree to travel to the various kingdoms of Kunlun to collect exotic medicinal herbs.
Upon his arrival at the South Sea, the local kings paid him their respects and submitted to him.
The breadth of his propagation was twice as great as before.
In the third year of the Longshuo era, he returned to his former temple;
all the scriptures he had carried with him had been taken northward by Xuanzang.
I intended to translate and transmit them, yet found no reliable source materials.

There are only two works: the *Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin* (one fascicle), also known as the *Sūtra of the Eight Maṇḍalas*, and the *Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Vimalamati Concerning the Paying of Homage to the Buddha* (one fascicle).
The *Atānātiya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle.
These comprise three sections in three fascicles;
they are essential, concise, and most profound, and should be practiced and studied constantly.
The śramaṇa Huize of Chanlin Monastery translated the words;
the śramaṇa Daoxuan of Fengde Monastery compiled the text and composed the preface;
[and] the śramaṇa Yaśobhadra.
In the Tang language, his name was Zhixian.
He was a native of Puling—also known as the kingdom of Haling—in the South Seas.
He was well-versed in the study of the Tripiṭaka.
In the past, during the Linde era, the śramaṇa Huìníng of Chengdu in Yizhou traveled to India to visit and pay homage to the sacred sites.
He set sail westward, and his route passed through the kingdom of Bolor.
He then translated it together with Zhixian.
One fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the "Section on the Cremation," in two scrolls, was sent via the *Jijing* (Conveying Scriptures) to Jiaozhou.
Ning compared this to the original in India.

Later, at the beginning of the Yifeng era, Liang Nanji, the Governor-General of Jiaozhou, dispatched an envoy with scriptures to the capital. In the third year, the Wuyin year, the śramaṇa Linghui of the Great Ci'en Monastery [received them].
He requested its implementation from the Eastern Palace.
The śramaṇa Divākara— translated into Chinese as Rìzhào (Sunlight)—
[was the one who brought it].
A native of Central India,
he had a profound understanding of the Eight Collections (aṣṭapiṭaka) and was extensively learned in the Four Āgamas.
His observance of the precepts was pure and lofty, and his scholarly achievements were abundant and excellent.
He was particularly skilled in incantations and thoroughly mastered the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*).
With the aim of benefiting sentient beings, he traveled to this country;
he arrived during the initial years of the Tiangong Yifeng era and remained until the final years of the Tianhou Chuigong era.
In the two capitals— at Taishōji in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) and Hongfusi in the Western Capital (Chang’an)—
he translated one work, the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, in twenty-two fascicles, and one work,
the *Mahāyāna-guhyakośa-sūtra*, in three fascicles.
The Mahāyāna-vijñapti-prakāśana-sūtra, one fascicle in two volumes;
the Mahāyāna-saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra, one fascicle in two volumes;
and the Avatamsaka-sūtra of the Buddha, Entering the Dharma Realm Chapter, one volume.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Universal Radiance Treasury Free from Words, one fascicle;
the Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Dharma-gate of the Non-Word Universal Radiance Treasury, one fascicle;
the Mahāvaipulya Siṃhanāda Sūtra, one fascicle.
*Mahāyāna-śatapuṇyalakṣaṇasūtra*, one fascicle;
*Mahāyāna-śatapuṇyavyūhalakṣaṇasūtra*, one fascicle;
*Mahāyāna-caturdharmasūtra*, one fascicle.
*The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Cultivation of the Four Dharmas*, one fascicle;
*The Scripture on the Great-Hearted Cundī Dhāraṇī of the Seven Koṭis of Buddhas*, one fascicle;
*The Scripture on the Most Victorious Dhāraṇī of the Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa*, one fascicle.
One fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī of the Supreme Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa for Purifying Karmic Obstructions*.
One fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Merit of Constructing Stūpas*.
One work in two fascicles titled the *Treatise on Destroying Attachment and Not Destroying Conventional Designations* (*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-arthakathā*).
One fascicle of the *Mahāyāna-pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*.
In total, eighteen works comprising thirty-four fascicles,
translated by the śramaṇa Candraprabhādeva.
The śramaṇa Huizhi was certified in the Sanskrit language;
by imperial decree, ten men of renowned virtue were summoned to assist in his propagation of the Dharma.
The śramaṇas Daocheng, Bocen, Jia Shang, Yuance, Lingbian, Mingxun, Huaidu, and others were certified in the meaning of the texts.
The śramaṇas Sīxuán, Fúlǐ, and others compiled the text and recorded it by pen;
Empress Wu personally composed the preface with her own sagacious brushwork to adorn its head.
Thus the teaching of the Buddha was glorified and transmitted for eternity.
The lay devotee Du Xingyi was a native of Jingzhao.
During the Yifeng era, he served as the Director of the Dianke Bureau of the Honglu Si.
Xingyi was proficient in the languages of India and also possessed literary talent.
Among those who translated and transmitted [the scriptures], many were selected for their excellence.
At that time, there was a monk from the kingdom of Kaśmīra named Buddhapāli,
who brought a bundle of Sanskrit manuscripts to the imperial palace to present as an offering.
The Emperor issued an edict for Huikai to translate it;
it was titled the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle.
[It was translated by] the General of Ningyuan, Dupo.
It was also certified and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra of Central India.
This was on the fifth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Yífēng era.
Regarding this Du translation, all instances of temple names and national imperial names were concealed and avoided.
Thus, the World-Honored One is the Noble Honored One;
the world is the realm of sentient beings;
and great power is the great destiny.
"Jiuzhi" (救治) means "to save and eliminate.
Having completed the translation, it was presented for imperial inspection. After the Retired Emperor had finished reading it, he looked toward Zhiyi and said:
Since these are the words of a sage, there is no need for avoidance;
Du Shi submitted this according to the imperial decree,
but because certain circumstances arose, he set it aside.
Later, the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha translated it in detail by imperial decree;
it is titled the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-sūtra-parama-vijaya-dhāraṇī*.
[The original was brought by] the śramaṇa Buddhataila.
In Chinese, his name is Juejiu.
He was a native of Jibin in North India and resided at Baima Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
Translation of one fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgatagarbha-bodhimaṇḍala-sūtra-viniścaya-artha-nirdeśa*. This sutra was recently produced; its exact date of translation is uncertain.
For now, with the intention of propagating the Way, my primary concern is to distinguish between the genuine and the spurious.
Since this true exposition is unerring, why should it depend on a detailed knowledge of the year and month?
The śramaṇa Buddhāpālita— translated into Chinese as Juéhù (Awakened Protector)— ...
A native of Jibin in North India,
he disregarded his own life to pursue the Way, traveling everywhere to visit sacred sites.
Having heard that Mañjuśrī resided on Mount Qingliang, he set out for it.
Having traveled far across the shifting sands, he came in person to pay his respects.
In the Jǐngzǐ year of the first year of the Yífǒng era of the Heavenly Emperor (676 CE),
he took up his monk’s staff at Mount Wutai and performed his devotions with profound sincerity.
Weeping with tears like rain, he gazed upon the holy countenance.
Suddenly, an old man emerged from the mountains and,
speaking in the language of a Brahmin, addressed Pāli:
The Master asked with sincere earnestness and deep compassion,
"What do you seek? Pāli replied,
"I have heard that the Great Being Mañjuśrī has hidden his traces upon this mountain."
Coming from India, he wished to pay homage [to the Master].
The Master asked,
"Teacher, did you bring the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* from that country?"
The sentient beings of this land commit many transgressions,
and even those who have left the household life frequently violate the precepts.
This secret method for the removal of sins is the Buddha-ūṣṇīṣa divine mantra.
"If you do not bring the sutra, what benefit is there in coming alone?
Even if you were to see Mañjuśrī, how could you possibly recognize him?
You should return to the Western Land to retrieve that sutra and circulate it here in this land."
This is precisely to universally honor all the sages,
extensively benefit all sentient beings, and rescue those in the dark realms,
thereby repaying the kindness of all Buddhas.
The Master took the scripture and arrived here;
the disciple shall now show the Master where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī resides.
Upon hearing these words, Pāli was overcome with boundless joy.
He then checked his weeping and prostrated once more toward the mountain.
In the brief moment he raised his head, the old man had suddenly vanished.
Pāli was filled with even greater astonishment and redoubled his reverent devotion.
He then returned to his own country and obtained the scriptures;
upon arriving at the imperial capital, he requested an audience with the Emperor.
The relevant officials prepared a formal report and presented it to the throne.
The Emperor, with profound sincerity, revered this esoteric scripture;
he subsequently issued an edict for Du Xingyi, the Director of the Guest Reception Office of the Ministry of Rites,
and the Tripiṭaka Master Sūryavarman to translate it together within the palace.
Upon completing the translation, thirty bolts of silk were offered as a dedication.
The scripture was then kept within [the palace].
Thereupon, Póli bowed and wept as he submitted this memorial:
He cast aside his own life with the sole intent of benefiting others;
it was his earnest hope that [this teaching] be spread and circulated.
The Emperor took pity on his single-minded devotion.
He then left behind the translated scriptures and returned the Sanskrit originals for him to circulate as he saw fit.
Pāli was filled with boundless joy at having obtained the scriptures.
He was about to go to Ximing Monastery to seek out the monk Shunzheng, who was proficient in Sanskrit,
and petitioned for them to work together on the translation.
The Emperor granted his request.
Thereupon, he translated it together with the eminent monk Yuan Ce, who was then engaged in translating scriptures;
the work was titled the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle. Thus, the fulfillment of the vow was completed.
The Sanskrit manuscript of the sutra was brought to Mount Wutai;
it has not emerged since,
and its whereabouts remain unknown.

Compared to all other translations, this one is the most widely disseminated. Regarding its preface, after the Yongchang era, someone compiled a record and collated various translation versions; the discrepancies in their dates are fully detailed as described in the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*.
The śramaṇa Divākara-prajñā,
also called Divākara-jñāna; translated into Chinese as Tiānzhì (Heavenly Wisdom).
A native of Khotan, his learning was thorough in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and his wisdom encompassed both the ultimate and conventional truths.
In the first year of the Yongchang era of Empress Wu’s reign, he arrived at the capital.
By imperial decree, he translated the scriptures at Weiguo Dongsi Temple,
from the first year of Yongchang (Jichou) until the second year of Tianshou (Xinmao).
Translated one work in two fascicles, the Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Merit of Image-making;
and one fascicle of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the Chapter on the Inconceivable Realm of the Buddha.
One fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra: Section on the Cultivation of Loving-kindness*.
One fascicle of the *Jñānolkā Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
One fascicle of the *Sarvabuddhasamāgama Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
One fascicle of the *Mahāyāna-dharmadhātu-aviśeṣa-śāstra*.
In total, six works comprising seven fascicles were translated by the śramaṇas Zhantuo (Saṃghadatta) and Huiji (Jñānajñāna),
with the śramaṇa Chuyi (Upagupta) and others serving as scribes.
The śramaṇas Fuli and others compiled the text;
the śramaṇas Degan, Huiyan, Faming, Hongjing, and others verified the meaning;
and the śramaṇa Shi Huizhi [supervised].
His father was an Indian of the Brahmin caste.
Having traveled there on a mission, he was born with innate intelligence;
from his youth, he was sharp-witted and proficient in Sanskrit script and language.
All translations produced by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara, Ti-yun-ruo-na (Jñānabhadra), Bao-si-wei (Ratnamati),
and others were certified by Zhi as the witness, while he was also commissioned to provide the oral interpretation.
In the second year of the Changshou era (the Guisi year),
the Master Zhi personally translated at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital one fascicle of the *Praise in Verse to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*.
The śramaṇa Śikṣānanda, whose name means "Delight in Learning" in the language of Tang,
was a native of Khotan.
His wisdom was vast and expansive, and his mind was dedicated to benefiting sentient beings;
he was proficient in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, as well as the treatises of non-Buddhist schools.
Empress Dowager Mingyang honored the sun of the Buddha and revered the Mahāyāna.
Because the old translation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was incomplete and its sections disordered,
she heard from afar that a Sanskrit manuscript of this text existed in Khotan.
An envoy was dispatched to invite him and to seek out translators;
Śikṣānanda arrived in Luoyang together with the sūtra in the year of Yiwu (655),
the first year of the Zhengsheng era of Empress Wu Zetian.
Translated at Biankong Temple within the Imperial Palace in the Eastern Capital.
This one work, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, consists of eighty fascicles; Empress Wu personally attended the Dharma seat and composed a brilliant preface.
He personally wielded the immortal brush to inscribe the title of this preeminent work.
The South Indian śramaṇa Bodhiruci and the śramaṇa Yijing together proclaimed the Sanskrit original;
it was subsequently entrusted to the śramaṇas Fuli, Fazang, and others to be translated at Bujiaoshi Temple.
It was completed in the second year of the Shengli era, the Jihai year;
subsequently, in the first year of the Jiushi era, the Gengzi year,
it was [relocated] within the Sanyang Palace.
He translated the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* in one work of seven fascicles,
translated at Qingchan Temple in the Western Capital (Chang’an) and Shouji Temple in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang).
He also translated the *Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* in one work of three fascicles.
*The Vaipulya Sūtra on Entering the Inconceivable Wisdom and Virtue of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle;
*The Vaipulya Sūtra on the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle;
*The Vaipulya Sūtra Spoken by Samantabhadra*, one fascicle.
The *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-guhyagarbha-mantra-sūtra*, one fascicle;
the *Subāhu-mudrā-dhvaja-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle;
the *Śatasahasra-mudrā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Spell for Saving the Face-Burning Hungry Ghosts*, one fascicle;
*The Sūtra on the Merit of Circumambulating a Buddha Stūpa*, one fascicle;
and *The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Four Dharmas*, one fascicle—this last shares the same title as the translation by Tripiṭaka Master Jñānasūrya, yet its wording and meaning are entirely different.
The Sūtra on the Ten Wholesome Paths of Action, one fascicle;
The Mahāyāna Awakening of Faith Treatise, two fascicles;
and the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-anuparivarta-sūtra, one fascicle.
*The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on Neither Arising nor Ceasing*, one fascicle;
*The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle;
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Stainless Pure Light*, one fascicle.
The *Bodhisattva-janma-catur-dharma-sūtra*, one fascicle.
In total, there are nineteen works comprising one hundred and seven fascicles,
transcribed by the śramaṇas Bolun, Xuanguī, and others.
The śramaṇas Fuli and others compiled the text;
the śramaṇas Fabao and Hongjing and others verified the meaning;
and Jia Yingfu, Attendant-in-Ordinary to the Crown Prince, supervised the translation.
The Brahmin Li Wuchan was a native of Lampāka in North India;
he possessed keen intelligence and vast learning,
being thoroughly versed in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings.
He was thoroughly proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit without impediment.
When the Tripiṭaka masters Ān-chen-na, Bodhiruci, and others translated various scriptures,
they never employed words of flattery or exaggeration.
In the third year of the Shengli era (the Gengzi year) during the reign of Empress Wu,
for the Silla monk Mingxiao,
at the Translation Hall of Fo-shou-ji Monastery.
A single fascicle of the *Amoghapāśa Dhāraṇī Sūtra* was translated.
The śramaṇa Bolun acted as the scribe and composed the preface;
the śramaṇa Mitaoshan [assisted].
His name in the language of Tang was Jiyou (Śāntimitra).
He was a native of the country of Tukhāra.
Having left home at a young age, he traveled through the five regions of India to study various sūtras and śāstras.
Among the Laṅkāvatāra and the Abhidharmakośa, this is the most exquisite.
Initially, he co-translated the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* with Śikṣānanda;
later, during the final years of Empress Wu’s reign.
Together with the śramaṇa Dharmagupta and others,
he translated the *Amuktasannāha-vimalaprabhā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in one fascicle.
The śramaṇa Añjingna...
In Chinese, he is called Baosiwei (Precious Contemplation).
He was a native of Kāśmīra in North India and belonged to the Kṣatriya caste.
Having left home in his youth, he made the practice of meditation and recitation his vocation.
After receiving full ordination, he specialized in the Vinaya-piṭaka;
furthermore, his wisdom and understanding surpassed his peers, and his learning encompassed both the ultimate (paramārtha) and conventional (saṃvṛti) truths.
In the second year of the Changshou era, he arrived at the capital of Luoyang.
By imperial decree, he was stationed at Tiangong Monastery;
this was precisely the second year of Empress Wu’s Changshou era, the *guisi* year.
In the second year of the Shénlóng era of Emperor Zhōngzōng, the Jǐwǔ year,
he translated at the Shòujì Tiāngōng and Fúxiān Monasteries one work in three fascicles: the *Amoghapāśa-dhāraṇī-īśvararāja-sūtra*.
*The Sūtra on the Merit of Bathing the Image*, one fascicle;
*The Sūtra on the Measurement of the Merit of Rosaries*, one fascicle;
*The Sūtra of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s Wish-Fulfilling Maṇi Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle.
The Mañjuśrī-mūla-ekākṣara-dhāraṇī-sūtra, one fascicle.
The Mahādhāraṇī-ekākṣara-hṛdaya-mantra-sūtra for the Age of Dharma-Deterioration, one fascicle.
One fascicle of the *Suvikrānta-śrī-paripṛcchā-mahāvaśitā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
In total, seven works comprising nine fascicles were translated by the Kasmirian śramaṇa Śrīnanda.
The śramaṇa Huizhi and others jointly verified the Sanskrit text, while the brāhmaṇa Li Wuchan translated the words;
the śramaṇa Degang and the Chief Secretary Li Wu’ai and others acted as scribes.
The śramaṇa Śikṣānanda was a native of Qizhou;
his secular surname was Zhang,
and his courtesy name was Wencming.
In his childhood, at the age of five or seven, he renounced worldly glory and cast off the finery of youth.
Thereupon, he extensively sought out renowned masters and thoroughly explored the multitude of scriptures.
He became proficient in both the inner and outer teachings, and attained universal knowledge of both the present and the past.

Having traveled as far as the borders of North India, his fame resounded throughout Mahācīna.
Our Emperor, gathering together men of virtue and talent, dispatched an envoy to welcome him.
In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, on the Jǐngchén day, he arrived in Chang’an bringing a vast collection of Sanskrit manuscripts.
Initially, he was stationed at the South Court of Kōfuku-ji Temple;
subsequently, by imperial decree, he was ordered to reside at Sai-myō-ji.
In the fifth year, the Ding-si year, he arrived at Bodai-in.

*The Dhāraṇī of the Most Excellent Mind of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva for Fulfilling All Wishes and the Method for Seeking the Power of Hearing and Retention*, translated by the Śramaṇa Siddhārtha. Translated orally.
The śramaṇa Asaṅga compiled the text and recorded it by pen.
Regarding the Sanskrit manuscripts that Vajrabodhi had brought, there was an imperial decree ordering them all to be sent into the palace;
because of this, he was unable to translate the various sūtras extensively.
In the past, the śramaṇa Wuxing traveled west to India; having completed his studies, he was returning east when he unfortunately passed away upon reaching Northern India.
An imperial edict was issued to welcome back the Sanskrit manuscripts he had brought with him.
Recently, while being kept and managed at Huayan Temple in the Western Capital,
Amoghavajra and the śramaṇa Yi Xing discovered several copies of Sanskrit sūtras there;
they were all profound gateways of dhāraṇī that had never before been translated.
In the twelfth year, he accompanied the imperial entourage into Luoyang and was stationed at Dafuxian Temple. Thereupon,
he served as the śramaṇa for the translation of the *Mahāvairocana-buddhotpatti-vikurvāṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra* in one volume consisting of seven fascicles.
The complete Sanskrit original of this sutra consists of one hundred thousand stanzas;
what has now been produced is merely an abridgment of its essentials.
Furthermore, he translated the Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra, one volume in three fascicles.
The Susiddhikara Sūtra, one volume in three fascicles.
Translated by the śramaṇa Baoyue;
received orally and transcribed by the śramaṇa Yixing, who also revised and refined the phrasing and logic.
His style balanced refinement and substance, perfectly harmonizing with the profound meaning.
In total, he produced four works comprising fourteen fascicles.
By nature, he was fond of tranquility and simplicity; he cultivated meditative concentration to delight his spirit and frequently engaged in Chan contemplation to encourage those who were beginners.
Out of compassion, he took it upon himself to guide and attract others without fail.
When people questioned him with doubts, he analyzed their inquiries without impediment.
The śramaṇa was named Vajrabodhi (the first syllable pronounced with an *shēng* tone; in the Tang language, it means "Vajra-Wisdom").
He was a man from Mālaya in South India—this land is called the "Country of Radiance"—whose kingdom was near Mount Potalaka, the palace of Avalokiteśvara. He was of Brahmin descent;
having left home to become a monk in his youth, he traveled throughout India.
Although he was extensively learned in both internal and external teachings, he was particularly adept at *dhāraṇī*;
within this single door, he was rarely equaled.
He traveled and transformed beings according to conditions, benefiting sentient beings wherever he went.
Having heard that the Buddha-dharma was flourishing and magnificent in Great China,
he set sail for the East and reached the coastal regions.
It was not until the eighth year of the Kaiyuan era that he finally arrived at the capital.
Thereupon, he extensively propagated the secret teachings and established maṇḍalas;
all were created according to the ritual laws and invoked auspicious spiritual omens.
The śramaṇa Gomyō (Saichō) held these secret dharmas in high esteem and frequently approached him to seek counsel.
With a single gesture, the Master pointed it out.
He then established an altar for him and conferred the empowerment.
One Practice respectfully received this dharma and requested its translation for circulation.
In the eleventh year, the year of Guihai (1023), at Zisheng Monastery,
he translated one work in four fascicles titled *The Ritual Manual for Recitation Briefly Extracted from the Vajraśekhara Yoga*,
and one fascicle of the *Saptakoṭi-Buddhamātṛ-Jñānadhātu-Mahāvidyā-Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
Translated by Īśvara, the chief Brahmin of Eastern India and Director of the Secretariat for Translating Speech;
received in writing by the Śramaṇa Wengu of Mount Song, at Dajianfu Monastery, in the eighteenth year, the Gengwu year.
Also translated: *The Vajraśekhara Sūtra, Chapter on the Five-Syllable Heart Dhāraṇī of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva*, one fascicle;
*The Essential Yoga Method of Avalokiteśvara Cintāmaṇicakra Bodhisattva*, one fascicle.
The śramaṇa Zhizang translated the terminology;
in total there are four sections comprising seven fascicles.
Furthermore, he appended new mantras to the existing *Sūtra of the Heart of the Dhāraṇī for Deliverance from All Suffering*.
The wisdom of Zhi held the *dhāraṇī* seal, and wherever he went, his efficacy was verified;

it was indeed this man through whom the secret teachings were transmitted. What was recorded in the previous chronicle has been compiled according to the original records; as for discrepancies that arose in the interim, I have never deleted or supplemented them. If one wishes to inscribe this on a wall, please follow the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, excluding only the locally compiled works, so that the remainder may serve as an authentic record.
